lines.text: Atoms are incredibly small, so we use a counting unit called the mole. One mole contains exactly six point zero two two times ten to the twenty third entities. This enormous number is the Avogadro constant.
Molar mass links mass to moles. H two O has a molar mass of eighteen point zero one five grams per mole. This conversion map turns mass into moles, and moles into particles.
Balanced equations give exact mole ratios. Two moles of H two react with one mole of O two to form two moles of H two O. These coefficients are stoichiometric factors.

Let's react two point zero zero grams of H two and ten point zero grams of O two. Converting mass to moles gives zero point nine nine two one moles of H two, and zero point three one two five moles of O two.

From the balanced ratio, our O two needs zero point six two five zero moles of H two. We have more than that, making H two the excess. O two is fully consumed, making it the limiting reactant, despite having the larger starting mass.

The limiting reactant defines the theoretical yield. Our O two forms zero point six two five zero moles of H two O, or eleven point three grams. The unreacted H two, zero point seven four zero grams, remains in excess.
If we collect ten point zero grams of H two O, our percent yield is eighty eight point eight percent. A major pitfall: smaller mass does not mean limiting. Always compare moles to the balanced ratio.
